WorkspaceMembersRecord.description:
Links a user to a workspace, one row per workspace and user (unique index). Fields: workspace (relation, required, removed with its workspace), user (relation, required, removed with the user), role (select, required: admin, member or viewer) and status (select, required: active or suspended). An update that sends an empty or invalid role is refused with HTTP 400 and a field-level validation_required error, so every row carries exactly one role.

**Only an active membership carries access.** Every membership branch of every workspace-scoped rule, list and view included, carries a same-row active-status conjunct beside its user check, so a suspended member gets a filtered-empty list, 404 on view, update and delete, and 400 on create, everywhere. Branches that grant on another basis stay ungated: workspace and record ownership, and the author and self paths. No branch grants on assignment, so a suspended member who is still the assignee of a task keeps no access to it. See decision:active-membership-grants-access.

**Viewer writes only on an assigned task.** A viewer keeps every read a member has, and the membership branch that grants each create, update and delete across tasks, milestones, decisions, documents, comments, projects, saved_views and task_subscribers carries a role-is-not-viewer guard on the same membership row as the user check, so a member and an admin pass and a viewer is excluded. A task assigned to a viewer grants them no write: they may not edit it, comment on it, react to its comments, subscribe to it or add subtasks under it. Admin-only branches are untouched.

**How a row is created.** The createRule is null, so no caller creates a membership through the collections API. A row comes into existence when the invited person accepts a pending invitation (POST /api/tracker/invitations/{id}/accept, see collection:workspace_invitations), which writes status active; when the caller already holds a membership in that workspace, accepting leaves that row untouched, so a suspended member is never reactivated by accepting. Every workspace create, through the collections API or a provisioning path, also gives the workspace owner a self-membership with role admin and status active. A membership created without a role is a member.

**Read.** The roster is open to the workspace OWNER and any ACTIVE member, and any user may read their own membership row whatever its status.

**Update.** The workspace owner may change role and status; an ACTIVE admin may change status but not role. Neither workspace nor user may change. Status moves only from active to suspended and from suspended back to active, superusers included; any other value or move is refused with HTTP 400 and a plain message.

**The owner row is fixed.** Neither the owner nor an admin may change the role, status, workspace or user of the membership row that belongs to the workspace owner, or delete it: each answers HTTP 409 with a field-level last_active_owner error. A change that leaves the row admin and active is allowed, so an owner whose row was member when ownership arrived can raise it. A superuser is exempt, so an operator can still repair a roster. Ownership moves only through POST /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/transfer-ownership (see route:workspaces-transfer-ownership), after which the row of the new owner is fixed and the row of the previous owner can be changed like any other.

**Delete.** The workspace owner or an ACTIVE admin removes a member, and any member or admin may leave by deleting their own row; leaving is not an escalation, so a SUSPENDED member may still leave. The workspace OWNER cannot leave: transfer ownership or delete the workspace first. A member who leaves or is removed has their assigned tasks unassigned (see decision:leaver-tasks-unassigned).

**Workspace scope.** A request that names a workspace (?workspace=) can view, update or delete a membership only if it belongs to that workspace; otherwise it answers 404. A request that names no workspace follows the usual rules.

**Workspace trash.** While the workspace holding them is in the trash, membership rows are frozen: an update or a delete, leaving included, answers exactly as an unknown id does for every caller, so a member can leave again once the workspace is restored. Reading them narrows to the set that can restore the workspace, its owner and an active admin, with no carve-out for a user reading their own row; every other tier gets an empty listing and the unknown-id answer. Nothing is written on the rows, so restoring the workspace brings them back unchanged.

WorkspacesRecord.description:
The tenancy layer: user, then workspace, then project, then item. Fields: name (required), owner (relation to users, required, removed with the user), priorities (json: the pickable priority vocabulary), default_project (relation to projects, optional) and trashed (date). A workspace is addressed only by its opaque record id, so name is display-only: renaming moves no address and two workspaces may share a name. A name made only of whitespace is refused with a 400 error.

**Access.** list and view are open to the OWNER and its ACTIVE members; a suspended member cannot list or view the workspace at all. create is any authenticated user: owner may be omitted and the server stamps the signed-in caller; a submitted owner must be the caller, and naming anyone else is refused with a 400 error; a superuser keeps the owner it submits. update is the owner or an ACTIVE admin, and an update that sends owner is refused, so ownership moves only through POST /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/transfer-ownership. delete is owner-only. Deleting your last workspace provisions a fresh one with its seeded statuses, labels and priorities.

**Landing and switching.** GET /api/tracker/me/landing names the workspace a signed-in user should open, as {landing: {workspace, reason, invitation}} or {landing: null} when there is nowhere to go. It takes, in order: the earliest-created workspace the user owns that is not trashed (reason owned); else the workspace of their earliest active membership that is not trashed (member); else the workspace of their earliest invitation that has not expired, in a workspace that is not trashed and where they hold no membership (invitation, and invitation carries that invitation id, because the user cannot open the workspace until they accept); else the workspace of their earliest membership that is not trashed, which by then is a suspended one (suspended). GET /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/switch answers whether the caller may open that workspace, as {workspace, allowed, reason, invitation}: allowed for its owner and its active members; otherwise reason is suspended for a suspended member and not_found for everyone else, the same answer for a workspace that does not exist, one the caller cannot read and one in the trash, so the route reveals nothing a workspace read would not. When the answer is not_found and the caller holds an invitation to that workspace, expired or not, invitation is {id, expired}, so a client shows the invitation to accept or decline instead of sending the user to their landing; otherwise it is null. Both routes answer a signed-in user, a request without one with 401, and a superuser with 403. See decision:landing-and-switch-check.

**Provisioning.** Every workspace, however it is created, gets its shadow project (concept:shadow-project), five default statuses, three core labels and, when priorities is empty or missing, the default priorities urgent, high, medium and low, from one after-create seeder. See decision:default-priority-vocabulary.

**Priority vocabulary.** priorities is a JSON array of entries shaped {id, name}, most severe first. A task stores the id of its entry (an empty string for no priority), never the name, so renaming or reordering an entry changes no task, and a name may carry any character, a comma included. An entry sent without an id keeps the id of the stored entry with the same name unless that id is sent on another entry, and otherwise gets a fresh server-minted 15-character id of lowercase letters and digits; a supplied id must have that shape and may not repeat. Every name is trimmed before it is checked and stored. Every HTTP write is validated entry by entry and answers 400 on a non-array value, an entry that is not an object, a blank or non-string name, a malformed or repeated id, a name repeated exactly, or any casing of the reserved token none. A CASE VARIANT of another entry is ACCEPTED: High alongside high is two entries, matching the binary-collated unique indexes of statuses and labels. An UPDATE may not empty the vocabulary or send null, because nothing re-seeds on update; a CREATE may, because the seeder replaces it with the defaults. Programmatic writers write repo-controlled literals and are not re-validated. A task write whose priority is not the id of a current entry, a name included, is refused 400 with code priority_not_in_vocabulary, while a task holding the id of a removed entry keeps it and stays writable on its other fields. No priority is the UNSET state, not an entry, and is always accepted.

**Trash.** The first DELETE moves a workspace to the trash; a second DELETE on a trashed workspace purges it. A PATCH that sets or re-dates trashed is refused with 400, so only the owner, with a DELETE, moves a workspace into the trash; a superuser is exempt. GET /api/tracker/workspaces/{id}/deletion-impact tells the owner beforehand what the workspace holds (route:workspaces-deletion-impact). A trashed workspace drops out of list and view for every caller; the owner and its active admins find it through GET /api/tracker/workspaces/trash and restore it with a PATCH clearing trashed. Once a day the server purges workspaces trashed longer than app_settings.trash_retention_days.

While a workspace is in the trash, the work inside it, its projects and their tasks, documents, decisions and milestones, with the edit history and subscriptions that hang off them, is hidden from every member, the owner and an active admin included, and frozen so none of it can be created, edited or deleted. Unsubscribing from a task stays available throughout. Its configuration is frozen too: statuses, labels, cycles, templates, saved views and the member list refuse every create, update and delete, and reading them narrows to the owner and an ACTIVE admin. Nothing inside is stamped, so restoring the workspace brings all of it back at once. Notifications about that work are the one exception: they are deleted when the workspace is trashed and a restore brings none of them back. See decision:workspace-trash-cascades.

post.description:
Auth required: an anonymous POST is 401. The JSON body names one workspace to export ({workspace, projects, collections}); workspace is mandatory and a blank or missing value is 400. projects and collections, when present and not null, must each be an array of strings; any other value, such as a single string or an array holding a number, is refused with 400 before anything is read. The caller must be able to read that workspace, as its owner or through a member row, or the route answers 404, the same existence-hiding shape a denied view returns. Routes bypass collection rules and the reads run in superuser context, so every per-collection read boundary is re-enforced in the handler rather than inherited.

**Scope.** projects null or empty exports every readable project in the workspace; a supplied list is intersected with the readable set and can only narrow, never widen. A narrowing selection also filters the project-bearing content (tasks, documents, decisions, milestones, labels, saved views) to the selected projects plus the rows inside the shadow project of the workspace (concept:shadow-project), which are kept by naming that container. collections null exports the default set; a supplied list is intersected with it.

**Data.** The response carries workspaces, workspace_members, projects, tasks, comments, documents, decisions, milestones, labels, statuses, saved_views, task_activity, task_subscribers, notifications, user_settings and users, and every relation field stays the stored record id. The graph is NOT closed: an item in the shadow project carries the id of that container, which is deliberately absent from the exported projects array, so an importer places those rows itself; exporting the container would undo its invisibility.

Per-collection cuts match the live read rules: trashed rows are excluded; a draft document, decision or milestone reaches only its author, the workspace owner or an admin; a saved view is included only when it is workspace-scoped or owned by the caller; comments and task subscribers are included only when their parent row is in the export; an activity row naming a task is included only when that task is exported, and the workspace-level activity rows that name no task, such as an ownership handover, are always included, so the export carries the whole audit trail of the workspace without a narrowed export gaining another project activity; notifications are the own rows of the caller, from any workspace, that the notifications list rule returns, so a dismissed row and a row about an item the caller cannot read, such as one in a workspace where the caller is suspended, are left out; user_settings is the own row of the caller only; workspace_members honours its own read rule. The users block holds only the accounts referenced by exported rows (authors, assignees, owners, actors and members), each reduced to id, name, avatar, verified, approved, created and updated; email rides only the own row of the caller, and password and tokenKey are never emitted.

**Attachments.** tasks, documents, decisions and milestones export an attachments array of the stored filenames on every row, present and empty when a row holds no files. Bounded: the export carries filenames only, with no file bytes, download URL or file token, so it is not a self-contained backup and an importer fetches and re-uploads the bytes separately; and it is a point-in-time read with no incremental or paging cursor.

Who may call: anyone signed in, a user or a superuser. A missing or invalid token gets 401; a signed-in caller who may not do this gets 403, or 404 where a refusal would reveal something hidden from them. An API key acts as its user, so it may call this too. 400: The workspace is missing or blank, or projects or collections is neither null nor a list of strings. 404: The workspace does not exist, is in the trash, or the caller is neither its owner nor an active member. Rate limit: the /api/tracker/ routes and /api/health together allow 300 requests per 60 seconds per client address (collection endpoints are counted separately); past that the answer is 429 with no retry header, so wait out the window. Superusers are not limited. Unless an answer documents another body, every error body is {"status": <code>, "message": "<reason>", "data": {}}; a validation error lists the offending fields under data.

Auth required; a superuser answers 403, because it holds no workspace. Returns {user, unread_notifications, workspaces} in one call (decision:me-route).

**user** is {id, name} of the caller.

**workspaces** lists every live workspace the caller owns or holds a membership row in; a trashed workspace is left out (see route:workspaces-trash). Each entry is {id, name, role, status, counts, capabilities}. role is owner for the workspace owner, else the role of the membership row (admin, member or viewer); status is active for the owner, else the status of the row (active or suspended).

**counts** is {projects, open_items}. projects counts the live projects of the workspace and never the hidden shadow project (concept:shadow-project). open_items counts live tasks, neither in the trash nor in a trashed project, whose status is in neither the completed nor the canceled category, so a task in a custom done status is not open, whatever its name. A task with no status counts as open.

**capabilities** is {write, manage, own}, the tiers of decision:role-tiers: write (create, edit and trash items, create and edit projects) for the owner, an admin or a member; manage (workspace settings and vocabulary, invitations, templates, project delete, purge) for the owner or an admin; own (change a role, transfer ownership, delete the workspace) for the owner alone. The flags say what the rules admit; every write is still decided by its collection rule.

**Suspended.** A suspended membership is listed with its id, role and status, so a client can tell a closed workspace from a missing one, but name and counts read null and every capability is false, because a suspended member cannot read the workspace.

**unread_notifications** counts the rows the notifications list shows with read false, each decided by that same list rule, so it always equals the read=false total of the inbox (collection:notifications).

Auth required. The workspace owner hands the workspace to an existing ACTIVE member by posting {user: <a users record id>}. This route is the only path: the workspaces updateRule refuses any submitted owner field, so an owner PATCH is denied 404 before anything else runs.

**Atomicity.** The owner check, both roster reads and every write run inside ONE transaction, so two simultaneous transfers by the same owner cannot both be accepted: the loser re-reads the committed owner and is refused with the ordinary 404, leaving its own target row unwritten. A superuser has no ownership of its own to be judged against, so it must name the person it believes owns the workspace now in a current_owner field alongside user, and that name is compared against the owner the transaction finds. Of any number of simultaneous superuser transfers of one workspace, exactly one can name the owner found; the rest, and any wrong name, are refused with 400 this workspace is owned by someone other than the person named as its current owner; check who owns it and try again. A superuser that sends no current_owner is refused with 400 current_owner is required: name the person who owns this workspace now, before anything is read, so a real and an unknown workspace id answer identically. A current_owner sent by anyone who is not a superuser is ignored. An operator may read the current owner first and send it as current_owner.

**Effects.** The workspace owner becomes the target. The outgoing owner gets a workspace_members row at role admin and status active whatever that row held before, so a suspended outgoing owner is reinstated, and the row is CREATED when none existed. The incoming owner KEEPS whatever roster role it held and its row is not written, because ownership lives on the owner field and the roster row records the standing a person holds beneath ownership. From then on that row can be raised to admin but not lowered or removed (see collection:workspace_members). So after a handover and a hand-back both people hold an admin row. In the same transaction the route writes one task_activity row anchored to the workspace (field owner, from the outgoing owner, to the incoming one; actor is the caller, or operator holds the superuser email with actor empty) and one ownership_transferred notification to each of the two parties. A refused transfer records nothing.

**Refusals.** An unknown workspace id and every caller who is neither the owner nor a superuser (a plain member, an ACTIVE admin and a non-member alike) get the identical 404 workspace not found, whether or not the body names the caller, so the route leaks no existence. Then: a missing or blank user is 400 user is required; naming the current owner is 400 the new owner is already the owner; a target with no membership row (a pending invitee included) or a suspended one is 400 the new owner must be an active member of this workspace, and so is a superuser naming its own id, which belongs to _superusers and can hold no membership; an ACTIVE VIEWER target is 400 a viewer cannot be made the owner of this workspace, because the read-only tier is not eligible to hold a workspace. A trashed workspace answers the owner and a superuser with 400 this workspace is in the trash; restore it before transferring ownership, and that cause outranks a wrong current_owner and a self-naming target; restoring the workspace makes the same handover succeed.

**Account deletion.** The sole owner of a workspace that has other members is refused self-delete; once the workspace is handed over the account deletes cleanly. A trashed workspace still counts as owned, so trashing it is not a way around that refusal. See collection:workspaces, collection:task_activity and collection:notifications.
